name: Printing A Sequence of Repeated Numbers (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that receives an integer N from the user and prints a sequence of space-separated numbers from 1 to N such that each number in the sequence is repeated 5 times.
code:
#Step 1: Read the integer N that the user enters
N = int(input("Enter the integer N: "))
#Step 2: Print N space-separated numbers
for i in range(1, N+1):  
    #Step 2.1: Print the i-th number five times
    for j in range(1, 6): 
        print(i)

commentList: Purpose: This line asks the user to type a value, converts that typed text into an integer, and stores that integer in the variable N so the rest of the program can use it.

Syntax and semantics: input("Enter the integer N: ") displays the prompt and returns what the user types as a string; int(...) converts that string into an integer value; the = operator assigns that integer to the name N.

Possible errors and misconceptions: If the user types something that is not a valid integer (for example letters, or a decimal like 3.5), int(...) will raise a ValueError and the program will stop unless you handle it. Note also that input() returns text (a string) — int() creates a new integer from that text; it does not modify any existing variable.

How it affects the rest of the program: The loop for i in range(1, N+1) uses the integer value stored in N. If N is 0 or negative, that loop will run zero times, so you may want to check N’s value depending on the desired behavior.

Best practices: Make the prompt clear, and validate the input. For example, use try/except to catch ValueError and re-prompt the user, or use input().strip() before converting. Also consider checking that N is positive if you expect a positive range.

commentList: Purpose: This for-statement sets up a loop that goes through each number i from 1 up to and including N, so you can handle each number in turn and repeat it five times in the inner loop.

Syntax breakdown: 'for' starts the loop, 'i' is the loop variable that takes each value, 'range(1, N+1)' produces the sequence 1,2,...,N (you add 1 because range's stop is exclusive), and the trailing ':' begins the indented loop block.
How it contributes to the outcome: By iterating i over 1..N, you ensure the program visits every required number once; the inner loop (lines 6–7) will then print that current i five times.

Common errors/misconceptions: If you write range(1, N) you'll miss N because the end is exclusive. If N is not an integer or is negative, the loop may behave unexpectedly or not run at all. Also don't forget the ':' and correct indentation—missing them causes a syntax error.

Interaction with printing: The loop itself only controls which number is repeated. You must make sure the print inside the inner loop prints values on the same line separated by spaces (for example, using print(i, end=' ')); otherwise, using plain print(i) will put each number on a new line and not produce the space-separated output required.

Best practices: Use a clear variable name (e.g., 'num' instead of 'i') if it helps readability, validate that N is a positive integer before the loop, and be careful with off-by-one mistakes by remembering range's exclusive stop.

commentList: You use this line to start the inner loop that repeats the current number i five times; for each value of i the body of this loop will run exactly five times.
You are calling range(1, 6) which produces the sequence 1,2,3,4,5 — the loop header must end with a colon and the following indented block is the loop body where the repeated prints occur.

Be careful: the loop variable j is not used inside the body here, so the values 1–5 are only serving as a counter; if you prefer to show that the variable is intentionally unused, use an underscore (for _ in range(5)). Also watch indentation and the required colon — missing either will cause a SyntaxError.

A common misconception is to think range(1,6) is required; range(5) would also run five times (0..4). Another pitfall is forgetting that print(i) adds a newline each time, which will not produce a space-separated sequence. To get space-separated output you should use print(i, end=' ') inside the inner loop or build a string and print once.

As a best practice, keep this inner loop tightly focused on repetition (use _ for the loop variable if you don't need j), and prefer constructing the output in memory or using print(..., end=' ') to control spacing so your program matches the required output format.

commentList: Purpose: This line prints the current value of i during each iteration of the inner loop, so you output the same number five times for each i and thereby implement the “repeat 5 times” requirement.

Syntax and semantics: print(i) calls Python's print function to convert the integer i to text and write it to standard output. By default print adds a newline after the value, so each call produces a separate line.

Potential error / common misconception: Because print(i) adds a newline, your program will produce each number on its own line, not space-separated as the problem asks. To get space-separated output you should use print(i, end=' ') instead, or build a single string and print it once.

Potential confusion about variables: The inner loop variable j is not used in this line; that is fine because the loop's purpose is just to repeat the print action five times. Do not confuse j with the value being printed—you are intentionally printing i.

Best practices: For the desired single-line, space-separated output use print(i, end=' ') inside the inner loop and, after the loops finish, call print() once to move to a new line. For cleaner or more efficient code, consider collecting values in a list and using ' '.join(map(str, ...)) to print the whole sequence at once.

Indentation and edge cases: Make sure this line is indented under the inner for j loop; if it's not, the repetition behavior changes. Also note that if N <= 0 the loops produce no output, so you may want to validate N before printing.

distractors.description: You might pick this because you know range(6) feels related to the number 6 and could think it results in five loop cycles, or because you forget whether range counts from 0. Step-by-step: range(6) iterates six times (0 through 5). If you use this line, each number i will be printed six times, producing one extra repetition per number. Again, there's no syntax error, so the mistake is logical: the repetition count is off. Compared to the intended inner loop that yields exactly five repeats, this line overshoots the count by one due to a mistaken assumption about how range(n) maps to the number of iterations.

You might choose this because you think writing 1 to 5 requires range(1,5). Step-by-step: range(1,5) actually iterates over 1,2,3,4 — that is 4 iterations. If you use this line, each number i will be printed only 4 times, so the output will be missing one repetition for every number. There's no runtime error, so the program will run and produce output, but it won't meet the requirement of repeating each number five times. Compared with the correct inner loop that ensures five repeats, this line miscalculates the number of iterations due to an off-by-one misunderstanding of the stop parameter.

You might pick this because it seems natural to use the same variable N you just read, or because you think both loops should be tied to the input. Step-by-step: this line makes the inner loop run N times for each i. If N is 3, each number i would be printed 3 times; if N is 10, each i would be printed 10 times. That changes the program's behavior so numbers are repeated N times instead of the required fixed number of repeats. There is no syntax error, so you might not notice the mistake at first. Compared to the intended inner loop that repeats a fixed number of times, this line uses a variable bound and therefore alters the repetition count. This is invalid because it makes repetition depend on N rather than producing the constant number of repeats required by the problem.
